pipeline.label: Sources
pipeline.description: Where data originates: operational APIs, event streams and external drops.
pipeline.why: Event streams like Kafka decouple producers from consumers and provide replayable, ordered input. Object drops handle bulk sources.
pipeline.alternatives: Point-to-point database extracts, nightly CSV hand-offs over SFTP.
pipeline.tradeoffs: Streaming adds broker infrastructure and schema discipline. Batch is simpler but introduces staleness and makes schema drift someone else's problem.
pipeline.code:
# kafka topic as the contract between systems
consumer.subscribe(["orders.events"])
for msg in consumer:
    event = schema.validate(msg.value)

pipeline.label: Ingestion
pipeline.description: Reliably landing raw data in durable storage, as close to source fidelity as possible.
pipeline.why: Landing raw, immutable data in S3 first means every downstream system can reprocess from source of truth — ingestion failures never lose data.
pipeline.alternatives: Ingesting directly into the warehouse; transforming in-flight during ingestion.
pipeline.tradeoffs: Raw landing adds a storage zone and a copy step, but gives replayability, auditability and cheap reprocessing when logic changes.
pipeline.code:
# raw zone: immutable, partitioned by ingest date
s3://lake/raw/orders/event_date=2025-01-01/

pipeline.label: Processing
pipeline.description: Distributed transformation: cleansing, joins, aggregations at scale.
pipeline.why: Spark scales horizontally across partitions, handles data bigger than any single node's memory, and offers one engine for batch and (with Structured Streaming) near-real-time work.
pipeline.alternatives: Single-node pandas, warehouse-native SQL (Snowflake compute), Athena for lighter jobs.
pipeline.tradeoffs: Spark clusters cost money and need tuning (partitioning, skew handling, memory). For small data it is overkill — pick the smallest tool that scales.

pipeline.label: Data Lake
pipeline.description: Columnar, partitioned storage — the durable analytical backbone.
pipeline.why: Parquet on S3 gives cheap storage, column pruning and partition elimination. Partitioning by event date aligns physical layout with query patterns and pipeline reprocessing.
pipeline.alternatives: Warehouse-only storage; row formats like CSV/JSON; HDFS.
pipeline.tradeoffs: Too-fine partitions create small-file problems; unpartitioned tables scan everything. Partition on what queries filter on, not on habit.

pipeline.label: Data Platform
pipeline.description: Where transformations become modeled, tested, documented datasets.
pipeline.why: dbt brings software engineering to SQL — version control, tests, documentation and lineage — while Databricks provides managed Spark compute and collaboration.
pipeline.alternatives: Stored procedures, hand-written ETL scripts, BI-layer transformations.
pipeline.tradeoffs: A modeling layer adds a build step and conventions. The payoff is maintainability and trust: lineage, tests and docs stop being tribal knowledge.
pipeline.code:
-- dbt: model + test in one place
SELECT
  customer_id,
  sum(revenue) AS total_revenue
FROM {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
GROUP BY 1

pipeline.label: Analytics / AI
pipeline.description: Consumption layer: dashboards, ad-hoc analysis, feature stores and AI products.
pipeline.why: Serving analytics from modeled, quality-checked tables means consumers trust the numbers — and compute is isolated from pipeline workloads.
pipeline.alternatives: Letting analysts query raw zones; feeding ML on unmodeled data.
pipeline.tradeoffs: A curated serving layer needs modeling discipline and change management. Without it, every consumer rebuilds the same logic differently.
pipeline.code:
-- mart consumed by BI + AI features
SELECT customer_id,
       total_revenue,
       revenue_tier
FROM analytics.mart_customer_revenue
